extractionNotes: EXTRACTION COMPLETE (as of the pass that added this note): this file contains all 28 Sub-Strand-year sections (Year One's four Strands, Years Two/Three's three recurring Strands each), matching the document's Scope-and-Sequence Learning Outcome total exactly. A prior save of this file under-counted Learning Outcomes at 29 (28 Sub-Strands each with 1 Learning Outcome, plus 2 on the very first Sub-Strand) against the Scope-and-Sequence table's stated 41; a full re-check of every Sub-Strand's own source pages found 12 additional Learning Outcomes that the prior pass had missed entirely (a second or third Learning Outcome row co-located in the same source table as the first, sharing that Sub-Strand's Content Standards without an explicit per-Learning-Outcome split): 1.2.1.LO.2/LO.3, 1.3.1.LO.2/LO.3, 1.3.2.LO.2, 1.3.3.LO.2, 1.4.2.LO.2, 2.2.1.LO.2, 2.2.2.LO.2, 2.4.1.LO.2, 2.4.2.LO.2, 3.2.2.LO.2 — bringing the Learning Outcome count from 29 to the correct 41. Each added Learning Outcome's contentStandards array is left empty with its own reviewNote (rather than re-assigning that Sub-Strand's existing Content Standards to it), because the source table does not explicitly state which Content Standard belongs to which Learning Outcome when a Sub-Strand has more than one — inventing that mapping would violate the no-fabrication rule, so all of a Sub-Strand's Content Standards remain recorded once, under its first Learning Outcome, consistent with the modelling choice already used for 1.1.1.LO.2 before this pass. Content Standards (38) and Learning Indicators (111) remain one below the Scope-and-Sequence's stated totals of 39/112 respectively; unlike the Learning Outcome undercount, this 1-short gap was NOT traced to any further missing node during this pass (every one of the 28 Sub-Strands' Content-Standard/Learning-Indicator tables was re-checked against its source page range and no additional Content Standard or Learning Indicator was found beyond what this file already recorded). The shortfall's exact source-page location is therefore still unidentified; a human reviewer should re-check the Scope-and-Sequence table itself (page 21, in-document count) against a full re-read of the 157-page source, since it is also possible the printed Scope-and-Sequence total itself over-counts by one for either field, rather than the extraction under-counting.

Document structure: SCOPE AND SEQUENCE table (PDF page 23, printed 'LITERATURE-IN-ENGLISH | 21') is badly column-collided in the -layout text extraction (numeric columns for CS/LO/LI run together, e.g. '2 24' where separate CS/LO/LI counts are expected) and could not be reliably parsed cell-by-cell; only the clearly-legible Overall Totals block was used: Content Standards 39, Learning Outcomes 41, Learning Indicators 112 (SHS 1-3), matching the prior inventory pass exactly.

Strand 1 'EXPLORING LITERATURE' (Sub-Strand 'General Knowledge in Literature') is confirmed present only in Year One; Strands 2-4 (Prose, Drama, Poetry) recur in all three years, each with the same three named Sub-Strands, consistent with the prior inventory finding.

Teaching and Learning Resources are printed after EACH Content Standard block in this document (not once per Sub-Strand as in some other subjects) — e.g. Strand 1 Sub-Strand 1 prints one TLR list after Content Standard 1.1.1CS.1 (page 27) and a second, different TLR list after Content Standard 1.1.1CS.2 (page 29). This is a genuine structural feature of this subject, not an error. Both per-Content-Standard TLR lists are preserved verbatim on their own contentStandards[].teachingLearningResources field (with its own source_TLR page), and also merged (deduplicated, in reading order) onto the parent subStrand's teachingLearningResources field for schema compatibility.

Content Standard and Assessment codes are frequently printed without the dot before 'CS' (e.g. '1.1.1CS.1', '1.1.1CS.2', '2.1.1.CS.2') — preserved exactly as printed, not normalised to '1.1.1.CS.1' style.

Learning Outcome 1.1.1.LO.2 (Strand 1, page 24): only a '21st Century Skills and Competencies' column of text could be located for this Learning Outcome in the extracted text layer; no distinct GESI / SEL / National Core Values text is visibly associated with 1.1.1.LO.2 specifically (the GESI/SEL/NCV column area for this row appears empty/blank in the -layout extraction, unlike every other Learning Outcome in the document). Flagged NEEDS_REVIEW on that Learning Outcome; guidance.gesi/sel/nationalCoreValues are null rather than fabricated.

Year Two Prose Sub-Strand 1 is titled 'KNOWING YOUR ELEMENTS' at its in-body heading (page 79), differing from Year One's Sub-Strand 1 heading 'KNOWING YOUR NARRATIVE ELEMENTS' (page 30) for what is otherwise the same recurring Sub-Strand across years (2.2.1 vs 1.2.1). Both spellings preserved verbatim; canonical 'name' uses Year One's fuller heading with the Year Two variant recorded in namePrintedVariants and flagged NEEDS_REVIEW on the Year Two instance.

Learning Outcome codes are sometimes printed without the separating dot before the final number, e.g. '2.2.1.LO1' instead of '2.2.1.LO.1' (page 79). Preserved verbatim in the raw-code context; canonical 'code' field uses the dotted form consistent with the rest of the document.

Front matter (PDF pages 1-24, printed pages i-22): shared SHS boilerplate covering the SHS Curriculum Overview, Philosophy/Vision/Goal/Rationale of Literature-in-English, Contextual Issues (subject-specific note on gender-perception bias and prescribed-text avoidance), 21st Century Skills, GESI, SEL's Five Core Competencies, Learning and Teaching Approaches, UDL, the Bloom's/Webb's DoK assessment framework, the Curriculum Development Panel list, and the Scope-and-Sequence summary table — not re-extracted per-node per the schema's Phase 5 design notes (document-level context, not curriculum-tree content). A stray/leftover 'Agricultural Science' title-block fragment was also observed mid-front-matter (PDF page 20 area), consistent with the shared production template's known cross-subject bleed artifact seen in other subjects' front matter; not part of Literature-in-English's own content.

Source-page attribution methodology: printed page numbers were derived from the document's own footer ('LITERATURE-IN-ENGLISH | n' / 'n | LITERATURE-IN-ENGLISH'), which is consistently offset from the raw PDF page index by -2 (pdfPageIndex - 2 = printed page) throughout the pages sampled so far. Because -layout text extraction of these multi-column tables sometimes reorders footer text relative to the body text it belongs to (a known artifact across this subject-PDF batch), individual Learning Indicator/Assessment page numbers within a single multi-page Content Standard block are assigned at the paragraph/code-heading level on a best-effort basis and may be off by one page in rare cases; this is a tooling limitation, not a content alteration.

Checkpoint 6 Phase 1 correction (2026-09-29): 9 Content Standards across 9 Sub-Strand instances were moved from the first Learning Outcome in their Sub-Strand's combined CS/LI/Assessment table block to the sibling Learning Outcome their own wording specifically matches (e.g. 2.2.2.CS.2 on 'personal and critical responses to narratives' matches 2.2.2.LO.2, not LO.1's 'themes and style in interpreting' topic, which keeps its own CS.1). teachingLearningResources: Templates (to guide learners organise their discussion)
Online clips or videos of films/skits and drama/songs

learningOutcomes.description: Use knowledge and understanding of concepts, types, importance of literature and literary genres in relation to oral and written literature.

guidance.twentyFirstCenturySkills: Collaboration and Communication: Learners work in mixed ability groups as teacher identifies their abilities and positions them accordingly to: share ideas with peers; accept constructive feedback on how literature mimics life; use appropriate academic language in the construction of their ideas; develop social inclusion skills and respect others' opinions, religion and cultures. ICT Literacy: Learners in groups, use available ICT tools, e.g., smartphones to search online for differences between written and oral literature. This enables them to: develop digital literacy as they explore varied art forms from online sources; be sensitive to inter-relatedness of the various aspects of life as portrayed in videos and clips. Critical Thinking and Problem-Solving Skills: Learners work in mixed ability groups to critically think and discuss the concepts, types and importance of literature and literary genres in relation to oral and written literature, learners are able to: critique to identify differences in genres applicable to life; relate their knowledge to make connections to real life experiences; identify and analyse different points of views and opinions in their discussions.
guidance.gesi: Working with others in groups in an inclusive way, cross-sharing of knowledge to promote understanding among groups and individuals leads to: respecting individuals of different beliefs, religions, and cultures; being sensitive to the inter-relatedness of the various spheres of life, groups, and individuals; being aware of personal biases and stereotypes; embracing diversity and practising inclusion.
guidance.sel: To promote holistic learning, learners' social and emotional learning must be consciously integrated in the teaching and learning process through the application of social and emotional learning strategies to ensure learners: Show empathy and cooperation; listen to peers; recognise commonalities and differences that exist among them to avoid bullying and harassing each other.

contentStandards.description: Demonstrate understanding and interest in Literature-in-English and make meaningful connections to text and life.

learningIndicators.description: Explain the concepts, types and importance of literature.
pedagogicalExemplars: Brainstorming/Talk for Learning; Think-Pair-Share: Share different materials, e.g., leaflets, manuals, textbooks on different subjects. Learners brainstorm to identify these as examples of Literature. Through brainstorming, learners in groups discuss the different meanings of literature to arrive at the meaning "literature is Life." Following this procedure: 1. Show a short skit, drama or film. 2. Guide learners to identify the issues in the skit, drama, film, songs, etc. e.g., who are the characters? What are the places mentioned in the skit? What roles do the characters play in the skit? Is the skit showing a real-life situation? 3. Let learners relate their answers to real life situations to arrive at the meaning of literature as life. Learners talk about characters, character traits, setting and issues in skits or films to establish connection to real life issues and draw conclusions to confirm 'literature as life'. Learners use language for academic purposes to develop confidence in communication. Based on the presentations, learners discuss the types of literature and its importance. Have them work in groups to enhance teamwork. Learners respect others' opinions and embrace diversity. Learners must use ethically acceptable language for academic purposes.

learningIndicators.description: Differentiate between oral and written literature.
pedagogicalExemplars: Talk for Learning: Through talk for learning, discuss written Literature and its types, using language for academic purposes.

Project-Based Learning: With the use of collaborative learner groups, review and explore knowledge on the different types of Oral literature from different examples of texts. Learners in groups, make a collection of an exhaustive list of types of written and oral literature under each major type. Encourage and reward creativity to enable learners develop their creative skills as they identify with examples in their culture through Oral Prose, e.g., Myths, folklore, Oral Drama, e.g., Cantata, concert party, Oral Poetry, e.g., libation, dirges, proverbs.

Collaborative Learning: In groups, learners identify the similarities and differences between oral and written literature. As learners work in groups, they should learn to respect individual differences and opinions and be good team players. Respect can be seen when learners communicate using ethically accepted verbal and non-verbal language.

dokDescriptions: Level 4 Extended critical thinking and reasoning

learningIndicators.description: Compare and contrast the relationship between genres in oral and written literature.
pedagogicalExemplars: Collaborative Learning: Present different genres of familiar written literature. Have learners interact with the texts, e.g., learners in group, identify literary devices and the elements of genres of literature. Learners learn to communicate using academic language as well as ethically acceptable verbal and non-verbal ways. In their discussions, learners must be conscious of valuing and working in favour of a democratic and inclusive atmosphere as they develop critical thinking.

guidance.twentyFirstCenturySkills: Collaboration and Communication: Learners work in mixed ability groups as teacher identifies their abilities and positions them accordingly to: share ideas with peers; accept constructive feedback on how literature mimics life; use appropriate academic language in the construction of their ideas; develop social inclusion skills and respect others' opinions, religion and cultures. ICT Literacy: Learners in groups, use available ICT tools, e.g., smartphones to search online for different literary tools for written and oral literature. This enables them to: develop digital literacy as they explore varied art forms from online sources; be sensitive to inter-relatedness of the various aspects of life as portrayed in videos and clips. Critical Thinking and Problem-Solving Skills: Learners work in mixed ability groups to: Identify and analyse the different literary tools applicable to different genres; relate their knowledge to appreciate varied literary genres; identify and analyse different points of views and opinions in their discussions.

contentStandards.description: Demonstrate knowledge and understanding in the tools of literary analyses.
teachingLearningResources: Templates (to guide learners organise their discussion)
Online clips or videos of films/skits and drama/songs

learningIndicators.description: Use the tools in analysing varied level appropriate texts.
pedagogicalExemplars: Project-Based Learning: Learners in small groups (mixed ability/gender), make a collection of examples from the different genres.

Talk for Learning: Through talk for learning, learners organise knowledge gained about oral and written literature by highlighting the differences and finding ways of making adaptations between the two genres. Relate the stories to written pieces using KWL charts, mind maps, presentations, etc. Through talk for learning strategy, learners learn to use academic verbal, non-verbal, ethically acceptable language. Have learners conduct discussions in an inclusive democratic atmosphere and organise work creatively using KWL charts etc. to present the concept.

In groups (mixed ability/gender): Discuss the examples of written texts developed from Oral literature e.g., Ama Ata Aidoo's ANOWA, Efua Sutherland's MARRIAGE OF ANANSEWA. Learners work as a team using language effectively and meaningfully. They must be sensitive to the inter-relatedness of the various individuals and groups as they appreciate the Ghanaian culture. Think critically to organise work logically. Learners identify genres of Oral literature and turn them into written versions to present in class. Create opportunities for struggling learners by presenting templates to guide them through guided practice. E.g. 1. I do - teacher models a task 2. We do - co construction between teacher and learner 3. You do - learner works with teacher as a guide 4. You do - learner works alone. Create opportunities for GATE learners by providing challenging tasks. e.g., Creative writing activities to develop creativity and inclusivity.

teachingLearningResources: Multi-sensorial classrooms (using different teaching strategies to meet different learning styles, e.g., kinaesthetic)

learningIndicators.description: Discuss short stories and novels of varied contexts for pleasure.
pedagogicalExemplars: Task-Based-Learning: Review learners' knowledge on features of Oral Prose. In task-based groups, learners are tasked to identify and present examples of Oral Prose (legend, myth etc) and their features.

Think-Pair-Share: Learners in pairs, brainstorm to discuss types of fiction. Share answers with other pairs for feedback. Pairing will help learners to respect individual differences. Again, communication must be in English Language as learners use ethically accepted language.

Talking Point: Through talking point, discuss the features of fiction using the varied examples identified. This is a whole class activity. Learners must be aware of personal biases, values and work in favour of a democratic inclusive atmosphere.

dokDescriptions: Level 3: Strategic reasoning: Compare and contrast the features of fiction in two appropriate level texts.

learningIndicators.description: Make a distinction between a variety of prose fiction texts.
pedagogicalExemplars: ICT Learning: In groups (mixed ability/gender), identify stories with varied themes online and share with other groups. This activity should give learners the opportunity to enhance their digital skills even as they play their roles in the team. In mixed ability groups, apply the knowledge on features in categorising the examples selected. Learners learn to develop participatory problem-solving skills. Share examples with other groups to critique. They do this by critically thinking of their inputs to get the right information and examples.
N.B: This helps to recognise the different learning styles of learners and create visual, auditory and kinaesthetic activities and learning opportunities.

learningIndicators.description: Examine characters and theme, and how they reflect context and society.
pedagogicalExemplars: Collaborative Learning: Learners in groups (mixed ability/gender), examine how an author creates plot and setting in a selected text. This activity will demand learners think critically to connect meaningfully with the text in the same task groups. Have learners present their findings to build consensus, innovate the work and present in print or on slides.

Diamond Nine Strategy: Appreciate the authors' craft through the use of sub plots with fishbone charts. Learners develop critical thinking as they apply knowledge which enables them to appreciate various authors' craft. In groups (mixed ability/gender), distinguish between the nature of major and minor, round and flat characters and their characteristics in selected level, appropriate texts with PEE template. Work in groups to develop collaboration to enable learners relate to and be sensitive to others and develop participatory problem-solving skills.

Project-Based Learning: Compare and contrast the use and effect of other elements of prose such as Foreshadow, Flashback, etc. in level appropriate texts. Learners think critically to apply knowledge to enable them compare and contrast these in varied texts as they reflect to present the right information. In sharing ideas and learning from each other, learners are encouraged to use academic language.

Structuring Talk for Learning: Initiate (whole class) discussions with the help of KWL charts, concepts maps to discuss and to review the meaning of theme. All learners will be required to participate, they therefore need to use ethically accepted language to avoid hurting the sensitivities of others. Learners can creatively present their information devoid of personal biases. In groups (mixed ability/gender), examine the development of main and sub-themes throughout the text. Present their work patiently waiting for their turn to contribute or critique as the case may be. In groups (mixed ability/gender), make general themes and turn them into thematic statements. Have learners present their work both orally and in written form.

learningIndicators.description: Discuss how the elements of language and style enhance meaning in fictional texts.
pedagogicalExemplars: Group/Collaborative Learning: In different task groups (mixed-ability/gender) discuss language devices such as humour, verbal irony, exaggerations, proverbs and contracted forms in texts. This activity will help learners communicate effectively and meaningfully in English Language and to value and work in favour of a democratic and inclusive atmosphere. In different task groups (mixed ability/gender) adopt collaborative learning and Inquiry-based learning to explore how the use of humour and suspense in texts, films etc. contribute to meaning, while examining the conflict, the pacing, the red herrings (clues in the stories that mislead readers), the atmosphere and high stakes which accentuates the suspense. Inquiry-based learning will help learners develop critical thinking and an inquiry-based approach to continual learning.

Building on what others say: Group learners in mixed-ability/gender to use carousel activities to discuss the role of characters in the development of suspense. Learners must be conscious to use academic language as well as using ethically accepted verbal and non-verbal language and respect the opinions of others.

Explain the features of narrative poems in context using creative pedagogies to create pleasure. Through inquiry-based learning, teacher reviews literary devices in context with learners to guide discussion on the beauty of language. Learners will develop their communication skills as they use academic English Language and develop an inquiry-based approach to continual learning.

Building on what Others Say: In groups, learners present the subject matter and themes of the poems read, and express their agreement or disagreements, on questions raised in respect avoiding personal biases.

Have learners work in same task-based activity to identify the similarities and differences in lyrical poems. Learners will develop respect for others as they learn from peers. They develop patience as they wait to take turns contributing their ideas.

learningIndicators.description: Interpret poems in context beyond literal meanings to show deeper connections.

Initiating Talk for Learning: Learners use think-pair-share strategy to read selected poems to make appropriate annotations as they collaboratively learn from others and respect their opinions while embracing diversity. Teacher elicits information from learners about the poem to get to literal meaning using mind maps, reflective journals. Teacher guides learners to arrive at varied deeper meanings through group discussions and presentations.
Inquiry Based Learning: Teacher asks questions to assess learners' knowledge based on what they have read and presented.

Talk for Learning: Teacher provides students with background information at this point. Learners use this background information with earlier ideas to appreciate unseen poems with questions like: Who are the voices in the poem? What is the setting? What ideas are being communicated? learningIndicators.description: Discuss the dominant theme in a poem and analyze in detail how it develops throughout the poem.
pedagogicalExemplars: Experiential Learning: Have learners brainstorm and discuss subject matter and themes, using a suggested format below. Example: Look out for recurring images/motifs/issues/ideas. Put together the related issues/ideas. Compose thematic statements. Distinguish main/dominant themes from subthemes. Learners develop critical thinking as they use the suggested guide to explore subject matter and themes in varied poems.

Building on what Others Say: Encourage learners to actively participate in the process of understanding the themes of a poem through thorough reading, annotations, discussions and research as they work in task-based groups. Learners can individually work while special activities are designed to enable GATE learners develop their talents.

Experiential Learning: Encourage learners using real life examples to relate the themes to real and personal experiences. Through reflection and journaling learners develop critical thinking. They are not required to share information in their journals. Based on textual evidence, the teacher incorporates moral and patriotic values to raise learners' awareness of values derived from the poem. Learners discuss the values learnt through reflection and motivate them to adapt to the changing needs of society through self-motivation and on-going training.

Task-Based Learning: Learners in mixed ability/gender groups are assigned different poems to discuss how authors use style to communicate meaning. Learners share their findings with other groups. dokDescriptions: Level 4 Extended critical thinking and reasoning

Collaborative Learning: Learners in groups, identify the aesthetic qualities of poetic elements. Encourage learners to identify and discuss some of the devices in context. Evaluate them to prioritise their effects/importance and their contribution to meaning. Learners assign literal or deeper meaning from varied perspectives to enhance structure and mood for effect.

Experiential Learning: Use role-play and classroom games to bring out the meaning and style of different lyrical poets/poetic structures e.g., difference between sonnet/ode. Discuss length, rhyme pattern/stanzas, musical/narrative. Collaborative learning will enable learners learn from each other and to appreciate the individual academic differences and work to help each other.

dokDescriptions: Level 4 Extended critical thinking and reasoning

learningIndicators.description: Compare and contrast how different poets experiment with the different poetic devices.

Learners select poems from different poets and compare and contrast their use of poetic devices. Groups share their work with the class. Individual learners select and practise this activity for personal development. Learners will use academic language to write their information. As the learners work in groups, they show respect and empathy.
